verses.translation_literal: And the snake was shrewd, more than every living thing of the field which YHWH God had made. And he said to the woman, "Indeed? that God said, 'You [pl.] shall not eat from any tree of the garden'?"
verses.translation_dramatic: Now the serpent was the most cunning of all the wild creatures the LORD God had made. It slid into the stillness and spoke to the woman, softly, as though it were only wondering aloud. "Did God really say it? That you must not eat from any tree in the garden?"
verses.directors_commentary:
The snake enters without announcement, as a creature among creatures: the narrator files it under 'living things of the field', the wild animals, and gives it one distinguishing trait, 'arum, shrewd. The word is not an insult. In Proverbs the 'arum man is prudent, and the word can praise cleverness or warn against it. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as saying the snake was shrewder than every other living thing, but 'not like a man'. Play it as intelligence without authority, a sharp mind with nothing to answer to.

Listen to the sound as well. Just before this, the man and woman are 'arummim, naked (2:25), and just after the fall they are 'erummim (3:7). My own reading is that the narrator sets these near-homophones on either side of the chapter's pivot, so that 'shrewd' and 'naked' echo each other: the shrewdness of the snake leads to the nakedness of the pair. Radak is careful to say only that the two words are spelled differently, wisdom-shrewdness with a shuruk (u), nakedness with a holem (o); the ear hears them as almost one word, and the text does not say it is deliberate.

The snake's opening question is a trap built from a distortion. God had allowed every tree but one (2:16-17); the snake says 'any tree'. The KJV 'Yea, hath God said' reads like a casual 'yes?' and softens it; 'af ki is an abrupt, incredulous 'Really? That God said...?'. The snake also says only 'God' (Elohim), never 'YHWH God', as the narrator does: the covenant name stays with the narrator, and the snake keeps God at a distance. Radak sees the same omission and suggests the snake would not be given the sacred name to say; Ibn Ezra says they did not know it. The verb 'you shall not eat' is plural, so the snake addresses the woman, yet speaks for both of them.

philological_notes.note: Shrewd, cunning, prudent. Spelled with shuruk, it is the 'clever' word (plural 'arumim in Job 5:12); the 'naked' word 'arom/'erom is a different spelling. The close sound to 'arummim (2:25) and 'erummim (3:7) is a wordplay I read into the text; the commentators note only the spelling difference and the pairing of two senses.

A compressed, incredulous opener: 'Really? That...?' Radak explains that 'af marks something added to earlier words, which implies a lost conversation, and that it can mean 'all the more so'. The question leaves out whatever came before.

verses.translation_literal: And the woman said to the snake, "From the fruit of the trees of the garden we eat;"
verses.translation_dramatic: And the woman answered the serpent, her voice easy, even a little proud. "We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden."
verses.directors_commentary:
The woman corrects him, and she is right. She gives the rule first as generosity: 'we eat', a plain present, nothing forbidden in it. Hold the line lightly. She is not frightened, and nothing in her words shows doubt yet. The verse ends in a colon in most English Bibles because the sentence is not finished; the exception comes in 3:3.

The KJV 'We may eat' turns a simple statement ('we eat') into permission, a fair reading of the context; the Hebrew verb is an imperfect and can carry either 'we eat' or 'we may eat'. Note also that she says 'the trees of the garden' where the snake said 'any tree': she undoes his exaggeration without comment. Radak hears her answer as 'it is not as you say', and Sforno hears her saying that they have no need to risk the one tree that God said would bring death. Both fill in motives the verse does not state, so play it as a plain, confident reply.

philological_notes.note: First person plural imperfect, 'we eat' or 'we may eat'. Hebrew does not distinguish habit from permission here; the context makes it permission. Her answer to the snake's 'you shall not eat' is the same verb, turned from forbidding to allowing.

verses.translation_literal: And from the fruit of the tree that [is] in the middle of the garden, God said, 'You [all] shall not eat from it, and you shall not touch it, lest you die.'
verses.translation_dramatic: "But of the fruit of the tree that stands in the very middle of the garden, God has said, 'You shall not eat of it. You shall not so much as touch it, or you will die.'"
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse the commentators argue about. The commandment as the narrator gave it (2:16-17) said nothing about touching; the woman adds 'and you shall not touch it'. Rashi sees this as the beginning of her fall, citing 'Add not unto his words' (Rashi on 3:3, with Proverbs 30). Radak gives a kinder reading: she is saying how much God loves them, forbidding even the touch lest touching lead to eating (Radak on Genesis 3:3). Do not play her as a liar; play her as someone who has made the rule her own, and in making it harder to break has also made it easier to doubt.

The KJV's 'lest ye die' is accurate, but 'pen' is weaker than it sounds: Radak notes it can mean 'perhaps/lest', where God had said 'you shall surely die' (2:17). So her 'lest' already softens the certainty. The same Hebrew word for 'tree in the middle' sets this tree apart from the other trees in the garden.

philological_notes.note: 'Touch' (to reach, strike). This is the woman's addition: God's command in 2:17 mentions only eating. Rashi and Radak differ on whether this is an error or a fence.
'Lest, in case'. A particle of apprehension. Radak observes that it expresses a possibility, whereas God's original word was an absolute 'you shall surely die'.

verses.translation_literal: And the snake said to the woman, "Not dying you will die."
verses.translation_dramatic: And the serpent said to the woman, quietly, flatly, with no heat in it at all: "You will not die. You will not die."
verses.directors_commentary:
The snake contradicts God by turning God's own grammar against him. In 2:17 God said mot tamut, 'dying you will die'; here the snake says lo mot temutun, the same infinitive and the same verb, with a 'not' in front. It is only three Hebrew words, and the shortest speech in the scene. Deliver it with no argument at all, since its force is that it needs none. There is no explanation yet; the reason arrives in 3:5.

The KJV 'Ye shall not surely die' is a good rendering of the structure and is often copied, but it takes the sting out of the repeated verb: the Hebrew pairs 'dying' with 'you will die' as in God's own warning, and YLT's 'Dying, ye do not die' keeps that pairing. The ending temutun carries a final nun: it is the paragogic nun, an added ending that gives the plural verb a slower, fuller sound. It is not the plural marker itself, which is the -u. The snake keeps speaking to both of them in the plural, though only the woman is addressed. Rashi reads the snake as first pushing her to touch the tree and then arguing that touching did not kill her, so eating will not either; Radak reads the snake as saying that God only frightened them so they would be careful. Both are readings of the motive; the text gives only the denial.

philological_notes.note: An infinitive absolute before a finite verb, which strengthens the verb: 'dying you will die', 'you will surely die'. The snake negates it with lo. The final nun of temutun is paragogic (added to a plural imperfect), not the plural marker, which is the -u before it.

verses.translation_literal: For God is knowing that on the day of your eating from it, then your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: "For God knows it," the serpent said, "God knows that on the very day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened. You will be like God himself, knowing good and evil."
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the snake gives a reason, and he builds it from God's own words. 'On the day you eat from it' (beyom akhalkha, 2:17) is God's phrase for when the death comes. Here the snake repeats the same phrase in the plural, and fills it with the opposite outcome: instead of dying, your eyes open. Listen for that echo; it is why the speech sounds true. The one thing he adds is the accusation that opens it, 'God knows', which is a charge of motive: God is holding something back.

The Hebrew keeps three promises in order: eyes opened, you will be like God, knowing good and evil. 'Knowing' (yode'ei) is a plural participle: the plural describes the pair, not God. The KJV 'as gods' reads 'elohim as a plural noun; Hebrew uses the same form for the one God and for gods, and ASV and YLT take it as 'God'. I read it as 'like God' because the verse opens with 'God knows', and I note the other option. The rabbis read the snake's point as a craftsman's jealousy: Rashi quotes the midrash that 'every craftsman hates his fellow craftsmen', and that God ate from the tree and made the world. Ibn Ezra and Radak understand 'like God' as 'like angels'.

Play it as the most intimate speech of the scene: quick, reasonable, offering the one thing the woman has just seen and not yet had.

philological_notes.note: 'On the day of your eating from it.' It repeats God's own beyom akhalkha mimmennu in 2:17, now in the plural. The snake replaces the consequence God named (death) with another.
'Like God' or 'like gods'. The word is formally plural and takes either sense. Rashi hears 'creators of worlds', Ibn Ezra and Radak 'like angels'.

verses.translation_literal: And the woman saw that the tree [was] good for food, and that it [was] a delight to the eyes, and the tree [was] desirable to give insight; and she took from its fruit and she ate, and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.
verses.translation_dramatic: The woman looked. And now she saw it as she had never seen it: the tree was good to eat, a pleasure to the eyes, and rich with the promise of wisdom. She reached out, took of its fruit and ate. Then she gave some to her husband, who was beside her, and he ate.
verses.directors_commentary:
Everything slows down here, and the Hebrew does it by piling up verbs: she saw, she took, she ate, she gave, he ate. The three reasons she sees are the three appetites: the body (good for food), the eye (a delight), the mind (desirable for gaining insight). The KJV has 'pleasant to the eyes' and 'a tree to be desired to make one wise', which is fair but turns 'insight' into 'wisdom' and the passive 'desirable' into an invitation. Radak points out that the first two echo 2:9, where every tree is 'pleasant to the sight and good for food', so the tree is no different in kind from the others (Radak on Genesis 3:6).

The small word 'immah, 'with her', is startling: the man is there. The KJV keeps it ('with her'), the BBE drops it. Whether the man stood beside her silent, as the plain text suggests, or was elsewhere in the garden, as Radak argues, the verb is as flat as hers: 'and he ate'. No argument, no reluctance.

philological_notes.note: 'Craving, longing, appetite'. Elsewhere it is used of strong desire (Numbers 11:4, 'they lusted a lust'). Here it names a delight of the eyes that is already close to wanting.
Hiphil of the root for insight or prudence: 'to give understanding'; or 'to become prudent'. Ibn Ezra relates the verse to her eyes opening.
'With her'. Read plainly, the man was present. Radak understands that she brought him some and told him what the snake had said, and they ate together.

verses.translation_literal: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked, and they sewed together a fig tree's leaf, and they made for themselves loin coverings.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew. They were naked. So they stitched together fig leaves, and made themselves coverings for the loins.
verses.directors_commentary:
The snake was half right. Their eyes are opened, but the text says nothing about what they see: it says they knew that they were naked. The verb is 'knew', not 'saw', and Rashi and Radak both take this as an opening of understanding rather than of sight. Ramban cites Rashi's reading and adds Psalm 119:18, 'open my eyes'. The text itself says only that they knew they were naked; why that knowledge matters, and whether it is shame, the verse does not say. Radak reads it as sexual awakening and shame; Sforno as knowing that the place of nakedness must be covered; Rashi, through the midrash, as the loss of the single commandment they had. These are readings, and the commentators disagree. Play it as the stillness after a sound, with no word for what they feel.

Note the sound: 'erummim, naked, answers the snake's 'arum of 3:1, and 'arummim of 2:25, almost the same word; my reading is that the chapter turns on it. Radak records that the word is written with a long yod here ('eirummim).

The KJV 'aprons' is the one place it softens: chagorot is a word for belts or girdles, the cloth worn about the waist, and I take 'loin coverings' from that. YLT has 'girdles'. 'Fig leaves' is more specific than the Hebrew, which has 'a leaf of fig tree', a singular collective; the fig's broad leaf suits sewing, as Radak notes. And nothing is said about the fig being the forbidden tree: Rashi and Radak report the midrash that it was, and that the Holy One never revealed the tree, and Radak lists other views.

philological_notes.note: 'Naked' (plural). Written with a long yod; it sounds almost the same as 'arum, shrewd (3:1), and 'arummim (2:25). The echo is my own reading; Radak notes only the spelling.

A belt or girdle, here a covering for the waist and loins. 'Loin coverings' is my own reading, supported by the YLT rendering 'girdles' in the packet and the root's sense of 'gird'; KJV 'aprons' is a guess at the shape.

verses.translation_literal: And they heard the sound of YHWH God walking about in the garden at the wind of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the face of YHWH God in the midst of the tree of the garden.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they heard it: the sound of the LORD God moving through the garden, in the hour when the evening wind rose. And the man and his wife hid themselves from the LORD God, in among the trees of the garden.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene shifts to sound. 'Qol' is both 'voice' and 'sound'; the KJV chose 'voice' and moves it to the foreground, but the Hebrew places the participle 'walking about' right after the name, so it is God, or the sound, that is moving. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban read the walking as belonging to the sound (Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban on Genesis 3:8). The verb is the reflexive 'mithallekh', a pacing to and fro. Radak adds that God made a noise beforehand, as a courteous person knocks before entering (Radak on Genesis 3:8).

'Ruach hayyom' is literally 'the wind of the day'. The KJV's 'cool of the day' is a reasonable paraphrase for the late-afternoon breeze that rises off the Mediterranean, and Rashi has the sun in the west (Rashi on 3:8); Sforno takes it as 'the will of the day' (Sforno on 3:8). 'From the face of' is more intimate than the KJV's 'presence': they hide from God's face, from being seen. 'In the midst of the tree of the garden' is a collective: among the trees.

philological_notes.note: 'At the wind/breeze of the day': the cooling wind of late afternoon. Rashi hears a direction (west), Sforno 'the day's purpose'.
Hithpael participle, 'walking about, going to and fro'. It modifies either the sound or God; Radak and Ibn Ezra cite Jeremiah 46:22 where a sound 'goes' like a snake.
'And he hid himself'. A singular verb with a compound subject, 'the man and his wife'.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God called to the man, and he said to him, "Where [are] you?"
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God called out to the man. "Where are you?"
verses.directors_commentary: One word in Hebrew: 'ayyekah. It is the first question God puts to a human being in the Bible, and the KJV's 'Where art thou?' is accurate but archaic; the voice should be neither angry nor ignorant. Rashi says God knew where he was and asked to open a conversation, so that the man would not be stunned by sudden punishment (Rashi on 3:9, citing Genesis Rabbah). Ibn Ezra and Radak compare 'where is Abel your brother?' (4:9) as an opening of speech (Ibn Ezra and Radak on Genesis 3:9). Sforno hears it as: you are not seen in the garden as before (Sforno on 3:9). Note that the narrator now says 'the man', not 'Adam' as the KJV does: it is a common noun with the article.

philological_notes.note: 'Where are you?', one word with the interrogative and the pausal suffix 'you'. A question that asks for more than a location.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "Your sound I heard in the garden, and I was afraid, for naked [am] I, and I hid myself."
verses.translation_dramatic: "I heard you in the garden," he said, "and I was afraid, because I was naked. So I hid."
verses.directors_commentary: He answers a question about place with a confession of feeling. The order matters: he heard, he was afraid, he was naked, he hid. Fear comes before the reason, then the reason, then the act that gives it away. The Hebrew is 'your sound I heard', the object first, which the KJV's 'thy voice' flattens. Note that he says 'naked' in the singular and uses the plain 'erom, not the fig-leaf loincloths of 3:7: either the leaves do not count, as Radak suggests, or the shame is deeper than the clothing (Radak on Genesis 3:8). Sforno compares this fear to Israel's after the sin of the calf (Sforno on 3:10). Play it without defiance: he is exposed, and he knows it.

philological_notes.note: 'And I was afraid', the same verb as the 'fear of God' that is later a virtue. Here it is plain fear.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "Who told you that you [were] naked? Is it from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from, [that] you have eaten?"
verses.translation_dramatic: "Who told you that you were naked?" the LORD said. "Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?"
verses.directors_commentary: God does not ask 'what did you do?' but 'who told you?', moving from the symptom to the source. Rashi paraphrases it: how could you know there is shame in standing bare? (Rashi on 3:11). The second question opens with a He-interrogative, 'hamin', and is a rhetorical one, per Rashbam and Radak: God knows the answer and asks to hear the man's reply (Radak on Genesis 3:11). The KJV's 'Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?' is accurate but clumsy. The Hebrew is knotted deliberately: 'the tree that I commanded you not to eat from, from it you ate', and the repetition of 'eat' shows the offence. Note the change from the plural 'you' in the snake's talk to the singular 'you' here.

philological_notes.note: The interrogative He plus 'from the tree'. A rhetorical question: Rashbam calls the He a 'He of astonishment', Rashi 'in wonder'.
'To tell, to declare'. STEPBible has 'did he tell'; the sense is 'who told you'.

verses.translation_literal: And the man said, "The woman whom you gave with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate."
verses.translation_dramatic: The man answered, "The woman, the one you gave to be with me. She gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate."
verses.directors_commentary:
Watch where the blame travels: the woman, and behind her, God. 'The woman whom you gave' puts the gift on God's side of the ledger. The verb 'gave' is repeated in the Hebrew, 'you gave... she gave', and the man only admits his own act in the last two words: 'and I ate'. Rashi calls it ingratitude (Rashi on 3:12, citing Avodah Zarah 5); Ramban says he thought a woman given as a helper would give only help (Ramban on Genesis 3:12). Sforno says the man attributes his guilt to his Maker instead of repenting, in contrast to David's 'I have sinned' (Sforno on 3:12).

The KJV's 'whom thou gavest to be with me' smooths 'immadi, an unusual poetic 'with me'. The pronoun 'she' (hi') is emphatic: 'she, she is the one.' The KJV's 'and I did eat' is correct but adds an auxiliary; the Hebrew is the short, bare 'and I ate'.

philological_notes.note: A rare form of 'with me' (more usual 'immi), found only in the first person; Ibn Ezra points out that it occurs only in the mouth of a single speaker.
'She gave', with the independent pronoun placed before the verb for emphasis. Repeats 'natatah', 'you gave', in the same verse. Rashi hears ingratitude; Radak: 'you caused it'.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God said to the woman, "What [is] this you have done?" And the woman said, "The snake deceived me, and I ate."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD God turned to the woman. "What is this that you have done?" The question hung in the evening air. She did not look away from it. "The snake," she said. "The snake led me astray, and I ate."
verses.directors_commentary:
The question is not a request for information. God already knows what was done; mah-zot 'asita asks her to give an account. The same words are Pharaoh's reproach to Abram when he discovers Sarai is Abram's wife (Gen 12:18, mah-zot 'asita li), and similar formulas of accusation recur at 4:10 (mah 'asita) and 44:15. Read as my own reading, not as a sourced claim: the question is an opening she can use, and she uses it only halfway. She names what happened to her ("the snake deceived me") and then states her own act in the plainest form, va'okhel, "and I ate." Note that she does not answer "what" with a description of the fruit; she answers with who and then with what she did.

The KJV "beguiled" is an old but fair word for hishi'ani, and it softens nothing; the Hebrew verb is the plain "deceived, led astray." YLT's "caused me to forget" misreads it, and BBE's "I took it" flattens va'okhel, "and I ate," into something with less appetite in it. Play the last two words quietly. Radak hears the sting in the reply: if she led the man astray, the snake led her astray, and God made the one who led astray.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of nasha', 'to deceive, lead astray', with the suffix 'me'. Rashi glosses it as 'made me err' and cites 2 Chr 32:15 ("let not Hezekiah deceive you") as the same verb. Ibn Ezra glosses it "enticed me" (pitani).

A formula of reproach. The nearest exact parallel is Gen 12:18, mah-zot 'asita li. Gen 4:10 (mah 'asita) and 44:15 (mah hamma'aseh hazzeh) are similar formulas, not identical ones. Sforno hears in this question a call to repentance for her too.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God said to the snake, Because you have done this, cursed [are] you from all the livestock and from every living thing of the field; upon your belly you will go, and dust you will eat all the days of your life.
verses.translation_dramatic: To the snake the LORD God said nothing of questions. "Because you have done this: cursed are you, set apart from all the herds and every wild creature of the field. On your belly you will go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life."
verses.directors_commentary: Notice what is missing: the snake is not asked anything. The woman and the man are questioned; the snake is sentenced at once. Radak and Rashi both read this as the judge declining to hear a defence from an instigator, and there is no reply to give. The curse is a formal pronouncement, and the word אָרוּר is the mirror of the blessing; the snake's 'cursed' (אָרוּר) echoes the 'cunning' (עָרוּם) of 3:1 in sound, a pun the English loses. The KJV's "above all cattle" is misleading: the preposition מִן means 'from among' or 'more than', so the snake is cursed 'out of' the animals, set apart and lowered among them, not exalted "above" them as a cold reader of the KJV might hear. KJV also uses "cattle" and "beast" for בְּהֵמָה (domestic livestock) and חַיָּה (wild animals); the pairing is domestic and wild together, meaning all creatures. In a world where snakes were feared and worshipped (Egyptian uraeus, Canaanite serpent cults, bronze serpent figures), a curse that makes the snake crawl and eat dust is a polemic against serpent divinity: this creature is an animal under judgment, not a power. "Eating dust" is the language of defeat and humiliation, as when conquered kings lick the dust in Ps 72:9 and Mic 7:17. Rashi and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan read it as the loss of legs; the Hebrew itself says only 'on your belly you will go'. Play the verse slow, with no heat; the darkest sentences are the plainest.

philological_notes.note: 'Cursed', the first of the curses in Scripture. Radak connects the word with deprivation, the opposite of blessing as increase. It sounds like עָרוּם 'cunning' of 3:1 and the pair has been heard as a deliberate pun.
'Your belly', used only here and in Lev 11:42, where the targum renders it 'on its belly'. Radak glosses the verb in the sense of bending low. Ibn Ezra says the root is uncertain.
'From among all / more than all': a comparative-partitive מן. The curse is relative to the other animals, not an elevation over them.

verses.translation_literal: And enmity I will put between you and between the woman, and between your seed and between her seed; he will bruise you [at the] head, and you will bruise him [at the] heel.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And I will set enmity between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers. He will strike at your head. And you will strike at his heel."
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech is addressed to the snake, and it is a sentence, not a prophecy delivered to a crowd: a hostility is put in place, and it runs between two lines of descendants. The word is 'eivah, enmity. Radak hears a reversal: the snake had made itself seem the woman's friend, and now the friendship becomes hatred. Radak also notes what is not said. There is no "all the days of your life" here, as there is in v. 14 and v. 17; the Hebrew gives no length for the enmity, and he reads that silence as leaving room for it to end. So do not play this as "permanent." It is between the descendants, and the text sets no duration.

The sentence turns on one verb, shuf, used twice: he will shuf you at the head, you will shuf him at the heel. The KJV keeps the repetition, "bruise... bruise," which is right; the BBE "crushed... wounded" loses it. The verb's exact sense is uncertain. Rashi takes the first as "crush" and ties the second to nashaf, "blow, hiss," because the two verbs fall on each other's sound. Ramban reads the pair as an advantage for the man: a blow to the head is fatal, a bite at the heel is not.

The KJV's "it shall bruise" is not a different reading of the Hebrew. The Hebrew pronoun hu' is masculine singular, and the KJV "it" follows the English word "seed" as a neuter collective, so "it" means "the seed." The Hebrew says "he"; whether that "he" is the line as a whole or one descendant, the grammar does not decide, and a director should not decide it for the actors either.

philological_notes.note: Enmity, hostility between persons; the noun for what an enemy ('oyev) feels. Radak reads it as the reversal of the love the snake pretended to have for the woman.

One verb used for both blows. Radak takes it as 'strike, crush' and cites Job 9:17 (asher bis'arah yeshufeni). Rashi takes the first as 'crush' and the second as linked to nashaf, 'to blow', hissing, because Hebrew likes the sound to fall on sound. The two blows land on head and heel.

'Seed, offspring', a masculine collective noun. 'Her seed' is unusual in Hebrew, which normally counts descent through the father. Sforno insists the enmity is not only between Adam and Eve themselves.

verses.translation_literal: To the woman he said, Multiplying I will multiply your pain and your pregnancy; in pain you will bear children; and toward your husband [will be] your desire, and he will rule over you.
verses.translation_dramatic: To the woman he said: "I will multiply your pain, and the weight of your pregnancies. In pain you will bring children into the world. Your longing will turn toward your husband, and he will rule over you."
verses.directors_commentary: Three things deserve the actors' attention. First, the pain: עִצָּבוֹן and עֶצֶב are the same root, 'pain, toil', and the very word is used for the man's labour in the next verse, so woman and man are sentenced with one vocabulary: their work is cut from the same cloth, and the bearing of children and the bearing of bread are both hard labour. The KJV's "sorrow" softens this; the Hebrew is bodily pain and effort. Second, "conception" in the KJV is wrong: הֵרוֹן means pregnancy, the long carrying, not the moment of conceiving. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the burden of the carrying. In a world of high infant and maternal mortality, where the woman's survival and the household's future both ran through childbirth, this is the most dangerous work there is. Third, תְּשׁוּקָה and the rule: the word 'desire' occurs only here, in Gen 4:7 (of sin crouching), and in Song 7:11 (of love), so its sense depends on context. Rashi reads it as sexual longing she cannot ask for; Ibn Ezra reads it as obedience; Ramban says it is a punishment that she will crave her husband despite the pain; and Radak reads 'rule' as the master over the servant. The verse is a description of the broken world, not a charter: the same book will tell of Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel acting with force against their husbands' rule. Do not play it as God endorsing the husband's authority; play it as a weight that now lies on the marriage.

philological_notes.note: An infinitive absolute with a finite verb: 'I will surely, greatly multiply'. Radak notes that this form intensifies the action; it matches the doubled 'dying you shall die' of 2:17.
'Your pain / toil'; the same noun is used of the man's labour in v. 17 and the verb in 'in pain (בְּעֶצֶב) you will bear'. The three uses, in vv. 16 and 17, tie childbirth to field work.
'Your pregnancy', not 'your conception' as in KJV and ASV; Rashi: 'the pain of the carrying'.
'Your desire / longing', rare (also Gen 4:7; Song 7:11). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban offer three different readings: erotic longing, submission, and an unhappy craving.

verses.translation_literal: And to Adam he said, Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat from it, cursed [is] the ground on your account; in pain you will eat it all the days of your life.
verses.translation_dramatic: And to the man he said: "Because you listened to the voice of your wife, and ate from the tree I commanded you about, saying, 'You shall not eat of it' — cursed is the ground because of you. In pain you will eat from it, all the days of your life."
verses.directors_commentary: The man is judged for two acts, joined by a single "and": listening to his wife's voice, and eating what he was forbidden. The first is not a crime in itself, since listening to a spouse is not forbidden; the offence is whom he chose to obey over the commandment. Sforno says as much: he accepted her reasoning that God was lying and jealous. The ground is cursed "on your account" (בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ), and here the pun of the whole story surfaces: אָדָם is made from the אֲדָמָה, so the man's sin falls on his own mother-soil. KJV's "for thy sake" sounds like a benefit; the Hebrew phrase means 'because of you' or 'on your account', and it is not a gift. The cursed ground does not curse the man; it makes his eating costly: the "pain" is the same עִצָּבוֹן as the woman's in v. 16. Note also "eat it": Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as eating its produce, as in "those who eat at your table" (1 Kgs 2:7), not eating dirt. Rashi imagines the ground yielding annoyances (flies, fleas, ants). In an agrarian world where survival was a matter of rain, soil, and the threat of failing harvest, 'the ground is cursed' is a sentence on the whole economy of the family. Speak it slowly: this is the one place in the chapter where God repeats his own prohibition word for word.

philological_notes.note: 'On your account, because of you'. The KJV 'for thy sake' sounds like a favour; here it is cause, not benefit.
'In pain, in toil'. The same noun as the woman's 'pain' in v. 16; Radak ties it to the heavy farm labour of v. 19, as against the light 'tending and keeping' of 2:15.
'You will eat it', i.e. eat its produce. Ibn Ezra and Radak compare 1 Kgs 2:7 and Isa 1:19.

verses.translation_literal: And thorn and thistle it will cause to sprout for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Thorns and thistles it will push up for you, and you will eat the plants of the field."
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence is short because the plot is short: the ground, which in 2:5-9 was made to sprout good things, now sprouts thorns. The verb תַּצְמִיחַ is the same used of the garden's trees in 2:9, so the reader hears the reversal: what grew to feed now grows to wound. The KJV's "thorns also and thistles" adds the "also" that the Hebrew lacks, and "herb" is old English for עֵשֶׂב, the green plants of the field, i.e. cereal and vegetables. This is not a curse of poverty but of a change of diet and labour: the man leaves the trees of the garden and moves to the plants of the open field, with its dry grasses and weeds that must be hacked out. Rashi asks the obvious question, how is this a curse, since plants of the field were already given in the first blessing (1:29), and answers that the curse lies in the thorns that come up with them. Ibn Ezra adds that thorns growing among the grain make the work worse. A field farmer of the highlands would have heard this as an everyday complaint.

philological_notes.note: 'Thorn and thistle', a pair; the second also in Hos 10:8. Ibn Ezra says they differ in size and mark the second as the smaller of the two. Rashi names them as plants that spring up among sown crops.
'The plants of the field': the green growth of the open ground, as against the tree-fruit of the garden. Ibn Ezra reads it as the grain that becomes bread.

verses.translation_literal: By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, until your returning to the ground, for from it you were taken; for dust [are] you, and to dust you will return.
verses.translation_dramatic: "By the sweat of your face you will eat your bread, until you go back to the ground. From it you were taken. You are dust, and to dust you will return."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the end of the sentence on the man, and it closes in a circle. Bread comes by sweat, sweat lasts until you go back to the 'adamah, and the reason is given twice, with ki, "for": from it you were taken, and you are dust. The man is 'adam, the ground is 'adamah; the sound has tied them together since 2:7, and here the tie is made into a verdict. The last clause carries the same grammar as the first: 'afar atah, "dust [are] you," and 'el-'afar tashuv, "to dust you will return." Say it flat. There is nothing to add to it.

The food is lechem, "bread," the work of a grain farmer, not fruit picked from trees. Radak lists what stands between the man and a loaf: ploughing, sowing, weeding, reaping, threshing, winnowing, grinding, sifting, kneading, baking. The sweat is from the 'appayim, literally the nostrils or face, the part where sweat shows. The KJV "sweat of thy face" is accurate. The BBE's "hard work of your hands" moves the image from the face to the hands and loses the body.

Sforno hears the sentence as the fulfilment of 2:17: "you shall surely die" (mot tamut) becomes "you will return to dust." My own reading, with no source behind it: the word 'afar here is the same word the snake was given to eat in v. 14, so the serpent's food and the man's end are one substance, and the woman and man are now, in one respect, in the same dust.

philological_notes.note: 'Sweat.' Ibn Ezra relates it to the root יזע, and compares Ezek 44:18 ("they shall not gird themselves with sweat"). Radak says the sweat is named at the face because that is where it shows, and a face sweats only from heavy labor.
'Dust, loose earth.' The man is called dust here as in 2:7 ("dust from the ground"). Sforno ties the clause to the warning of 2:17. The link to the snake's dust in v. 14 is my own reading.
Pual, 'you were taken.' The passive does not name who took. It is repeated in v. 23 (luqqach misham).

verses.translation_literal: And the man called the name of his wife Chavvah, for she was the mother of all living.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the man gave his wife a name. He called her Eve, the living one, because she had become the mother of every living thing that would be born of her.
verses.directors_commentary:
A name given right after the sentences, and given by the man. Radak offers two readings. First, this is the name he gave her when she was brought to him, as he named the animals, a personal name set beside the common noun 'ishah, "woman," of 2:23. Second, the name came after the eating: the fruit brought a new desire and the knowledge that they would have children, and so he calls her "mother." Either way the Hebrew says only that he called her this "for she was the mother of all living"; the order of events is left to the reader. My own reading, not Radak's: spoken straight after "to dust you will return," a name that means life is an answer in the same breath. Play it as a man who has just heard that he will die choosing a word that looks forward.

The name is Chavvah, and the sound is close to the root for "live." Rashi says it falls on the word chayyah, "she who gives life to her children." Ibn Ezra notes that vav and yod swap places in Hebrew. Radak adds that the name was chosen as Chavvah rather than chayyah to keep it apart from chayyah, "wild animal." The KJV and BBE both transliterate "Eve" and lose the sound link to chai, "living"; a reader of the English never hears the pun.

The word chai, "living," Radak glosses as "speaking," that is, people, as in "let all flesh bless" (Ps 145:21). Ibn Ezra also reads it as human beings. Sforno: she alone has the title because she was first.

philological_notes.note: The name sounds like the root for 'live.' Rashi says the name falls on the word chayyah, because she gives life to her offspring. Ibn Ezra explains the vav for yod; Radak says it was chosen to distinguish her from chayyah, 'animal.'
'Mother of every living one.' Radak: chai means a speaking being, so human beings; Sforno: she is the only one called this, as the first.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God made for Adam and for his wife tunics of skin, and clothed them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God made garments for the man and for his wife, long tunics of skin, and he clothed them.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet verse after four harsh ones. Two verbs, no speech: he made, and he clothed them. The first verb is 'asah, "made," the same as in v. 13 and v. 14; the second is hiphil, "caused them to put on." The garment is a kotnet, the tunic worn against the body, not the fig-leaf loincloths of v. 7. Rashbam says it covers the whole body.

The KJV "Unto Adam also and to his wife" adds "also," which has no Hebrew behind it, and "coats" is an archaic word for tunics. The BBE's "for their clothing" drops the second verb, vayyalbishem, so that God no longer clothes them.

The materials were argued. Rashi gives two opinions: something smooth as a fingernail, stuck to their skin, or something that comes from skin, namely hare's wool, soft and warm. Radak records the dispute between Rav and Shmuel: one says "a thing from the skin," the other "a thing the skin benefits from," and he names linen for the second. He also lists the view that the skin came from the serpent, and that from an animal sacrificed; he himself says there is no need to ask, since God commanded and it was. Ibn Ezra says we should simply believe that God made them tunics of skin. Sforno's reading: it was done without the man's effort, so he would not think himself improved by what he later made for himself.

philological_notes.note: 'Tunics of skin' ('or with ayin, skin). Rashi lists a smooth, nail-like growth on their skin or hare's wool; Radak records Rav and Shmuel (a thing from skin, or linen) and the other views he rejects as unnecessary.
Hiphil, 'he caused them to wear', 'he clothed them.' The second action is God's own, after the making; Sforno says he clothed them so they would not be sent out naked.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God said, Behold, the man has become like one of us, in knowing good and evil; and now, lest he stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat and live forever —
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God said, "See, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now — he must not reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever."
verses.directors_commentary: The verse breaks off. "Lest he stretch out his hand, and take, and eat, and live forever..." and the sentence never says what must be done; the next verse supplies it with action. The Hebrew grammar of פֶּן ("lest") leaves the fear hanging, and an actor should let it hang. KJV, ASV and Webster close the sentence with a colon or dash and keep this suspension; BBE and others smooth it over. The first half is full of irony. The snake had promised, "you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (3:5); here God confirms it with a bitter "behold" (הֵן), and in the same breath says "like one of us". The plural puzzles every reader: Rashi sees the man as unique below as God is unique above; Onkelos says the man is alone in the world in knowing good and evil; Radak and Ibn Ezra say God includes the angels, as in 1:26 ("let us make"). I follow no single view. The KJV's "is become" is a normal old perfect; modern English says "has become". The verb "stretch out his hand" (שלח יד) is the same gesture as the woman's grasp in 3:6, now imagined for the other tree. The second tree, the tree of life, was never forbidden: Radak notes that the man was originally free to eat of it, and what changes is that, having crossed the line, he must not eat of it. The point is to deny him an unending life in this state, not to punish him again. In a world where kings sought deathlessness (Gilgamesh looked for a plant of life and lost it to a snake), a story that ends with human mortality accepted would have been heard with a certain recognition.

philological_notes.note: 'Like one of us.' The first-person plural is read as God with the angels (Ibn Ezra, Radak) or, in Onkelos and Rashi, as 'unique in his realm as I am in mine'. I leave it as 'one of us'.
'Lest he stretch out': the clause opens a fear that is never finished with a main verb, so the verse breaks off. The next verse supplies the answer.
'Forever', or 'for a long time'; Radak glosses it as 'a long time' as in Exod 21:6, yet here the context is deathlessness.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God sent him out of the garden of Eden, out to the ground, to work the ground from which he had been taken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is shillach, "sent out," and the next verse uses a harsher one, vayegaresh, "drove out." Ibn Ezra and Radak both say that shillach followed by min, "from," is a sending of expulsion, as in Jer 15:1 (shallach me'al panai, "send them out of my sight"); Sforno says it means he commanded him to go. Play it as an order, not an invitation.

The work is la'avod 'et-ha'adamah, "to serve the ground"; it is the task of 2:5 and 2:15 (le'ovdah), now taken up outside. Radak reads it as the hard work the man earned by refusing the easy work in the garden. The closing words, 'asher luqqach misham, "from which he was taken," repeat 3:19 (and 2:7): the origin that was a promise of kinship in the creation story is now the place where he must labour and where he will return. The KJV adds "Therefore," which is not in the Hebrew; the verse begins only with "and." The singular "him" is the man, 'adam; the woman is not named here.

philological_notes.note: Piel, 'and he sent him away.' Ibn Ezra and Radak read the Piel with min as an expulsion, comparing Jer 15:1; Ibn Ezra rejects the view that it is a gentle word of honor.
'To serve, work, till.' The same verb as in 2:5 and 2:15. Radak: hard labor, in place of the easy work in the garden.

verses.translation_literal: And he drove out the man, and he made dwell, to the east of the garden of Eden, the cherubim, and the flame of the sword that turns itself, to guard the way of the tree of life.
verses.translation_dramatic: He drove the man out. And at the east of the garden of Eden he set the cherubim, and a sword of flame that turned and turned, to guard the way to the tree of life.
verses.directors_commentary: The chapter ends not with the man but with the guards. The verb is stronger now: וַיְגָרֶשׁ, "drove out", the word used of casting out an unwanted person or an enemy, as in Exod 12:39 and Gen 21:10. The KJV has "drove out" here and "sent forth" in v. 23, and that difference is faithful to the Hebrew; the ASV also keeps it. KJV's "Cherubims" is a double plural: כְּרֻבִים is already plural, 'cherubim'. These are not the plump winged children of later art. In the Near East, a kĕrûb was a winged guardian, a composite animal with a human face, set at gates and thrones; the temple's doors in 1 Kgs 6 and the ark-cover in Exod 25 carry the same figures, so the first audience saw Eden as a sanctuary whose entrance faces east, as the later temple does. Rashi calls them angels of destruction; Radak treats the whole scene as a vision meant to frighten and prompt return. The verb וַיַּשְׁכֵּן, 'he made dwell', is the same root as 'tabernacle' (מִשְׁכָּן); I note the link as my own reading, without making it a claim. The "flame of the sword" is a blade of fire that keeps turning (הַמִּתְהַפֶּכֶת, a reflexive: it turns itself over and over), whereas the KJV's "which turned every way" suggests a direction rather than a motion. The guard is posted at the way to the tree of life, not at the garden as a whole: the tree is what is protected. The text gives no comfort about any return. End on stillness and heat: a gate with fire in it.

philological_notes.note: 'The cherubim': winged guardian figures, here plural already, so KJV 'Cherubims' is a double plural. Rashi calls them 'angels of destruction'; Radak describes the scene as a vision meant to frighten.

'The flame of the sword that keeps turning itself': הִתְהַפֵּךְ is the reflexive (hithpael) of 'to turn', a blade of fire that rotates. Radak says 'flame' is a sight, not a body; Rashi relates it to the Aramaic for 'sharpness'.
Hiphil of שכן: 'he made dwell, settled'. The same root as mishkan 'tabernacle'; my own observation, not sourced to the commentators.
'From/at the east'. Rashi: east of the garden, outside it. Radak: the garden's entrance faced east.

events.title: The serpent questions the woman about the forbidden tree
events.narrative_summary: The serpent, shrewder than any wild animal, asks the woman whether God forbade every tree. She says only the tree in the middle is forbidden, even to touch. The serpent says they will not die and that God knows their eyes will open and they will be like God.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word links this scene to Gen 2:25; it follows the scene of the man and woman naked and unashamed, so it is anchored on the END of evt.gen_2.man_speaks_one_flesh with no offset. The gap is unstated, so the margin is a wide one year and the tier MACRO_ERA. A conversation of a few verses: about ten minutes.

events.title: The woman eats the fruit and gives it to her husband
events.narrative_summary: The woman sees that the tree is good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable for wisdom. She takes some fruit, eats, and gives it to her husband, who is with her, and he eats.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Narrated continuously after the serpent's speech (wayyiqtol chain, 3:6), so it starts at the END of the dialogue with no offset. Margin one hour to allow for the woman's looking and deliberating; duration ten minutes.

events.title: Their eyes are opened and they sew fig-leaf loincloths
events.narrative_summary: The eyes of both are opened and they know they are naked. They sew fig leaves together and make loincloths for themselves.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediate consequence of eating (3:7, 'and the eyes of both were opened'), starting at the END of the eating. Sewing leaves is estimated at an hour; margin ten minutes for the opening itself.

events.title: They hear God walking in the garden and hide among the trees
events.narrative_summary: The man and his wife hear the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the wind of the day, and hide from him among the trees.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'At the wind of the day' (lěruaḥ hayyom, 3:8): Rashi reads the evening west wind, when the sun is in the west, and says they sinned in the tenth hour; Radak reads the evening cool. Hence BEIN_HAARBAYIM (17:30). Anchored on the END of the aprons scene, snapping to the first such hour at or after it; the text does not say it is the same day, so the margin is 12 hours. Tier DIURNAL_HOUR for the hour marker.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: In the wind of the day

events.title: God calls the man and questions both about the fruit
events.narrative_summary: God calls to the man, 'Where are you?' The man says he was afraid because he was naked; God asks who told him and whether he ate. The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: God's call follows their hiding directly (3:9, 'and he called'), so it starts at the END of the hiding scene. Five verses of questions and answers: about thirty minutes; margin one hour. Part of the same evening, so DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: God curses the serpent and sets enmity with the woman's offspring
events.narrative_summary: Because it did this, God curses the serpent above all animals: it will go on its belly and eat dust all its life. He puts enmity between it and the woman, and between their offspring: he will strike its head, and it will strike his heel.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The first sentence follows the questioning (3:14, 'because you did this'), in the order serpent, woman, man. Starts at the END of the questioning; a short pronouncement, about five minutes.

events.title: God multiplies the woman's pain in childbearing
events.narrative_summary: God tells the woman he will greatly increase her pain and her pregnancy; she will bear children in pain, her desire will be for her husband, and he will rule over her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Next in the series of sentences (3:16); starts at the END of the curse on the serpent. About five minutes; margin thirty minutes.

events.title: God curses the ground and sentences the man to toil until he returns to dust
events.narrative_summary: Because the man listened to his wife and ate, God curses the ground: it will yield thorns and thistles, and he will eat bread by the sweat of his face until he returns to the dust from which he was taken.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Last of the three sentences (3:17-19); starts at the END of the sentence on the woman. About ten minutes; margin thirty minutes.

events.title: The man names his wife Eve, mother of all the living
events.narrative_summary: The man calls his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 3:20 is narrated after the sentences and before the clothing, so it is ordered after evt.gen_3.sentence_man with no stated gap. The naming could be at any point in the same scene or soon after, hence a one-day margin; a few minutes of duration.

events.title: God makes skin garments and clothes the man and his wife
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God makes garments of skin for the man and his wife and clothes them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Narrated after the naming (3:21), no time word; starts at the END of evt.gen_3.eve_named. An hour for the making and dressing; one-day margin because the gap is unstated.

events.title: God says the man must not take also from the tree of life
events.narrative_summary: God says that the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil, and fears that he might reach out, take also from the tree of life, eat and live for ever.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech that leads directly to the expulsion (3:22-23, 'and he sent him out'); starts at the END of the clothing. About ten minutes; margin one hour.

events.title: God drives the man out of Eden and posts cherubim at the east
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God sends the man out of the garden of Eden to till the ground from which he was taken. He drives him out and stations cherubim and a whirling flaming sword east of the garden to guard the way to the tree of life.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately follows God's speech (3:23, 'and he sent him out'); starts at the END of evt.gen_3.tree_of_life_concern. An hour to send them out and place the guards; margin one hour.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The man says he hid because he was afraid, being naked, a knowledge that came with the opening of their eyes (3:7, 3:10).
Eating the fruit is followed at once by the opening of their eyes and the knowledge of nakedness (3:6-7).
God sentences the man 'because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree' (3:17), pointing back to the eating of 3:6.
God's sentence on the woman follows 'What is this you have done?' and her admission 'I ate' (3:13, 3:16); the text gives no 'because' here, so the link is inferred.
God speaks because the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil, through eating (3:22).
God calls 'Where are you?' to the man who is hiding from him (3:8-9).
The serpent's deception, which the woman names ('the serpent deceived me', 3:13), is why God curses it 'because you have done this' (3:14).
The serpent's assurance that they will not die and will become like God leads the woman to take the fruit (3:4-6).
God's fear that the man might also eat of the tree of life leads him to send him out of the garden (3:22-23).

aliases: the flame of the whirling sword
entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'the flame of the sword that turns itself', a blade or blaze that rotates.
entities.summary_bio: A flame or sword that turns every way, set with the cherubim east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.
Tunics made by the LORD God for the man and his wife and put on them, replacing their fig-leaf coverings before they leave Eden.

entities.etymology_meaning: Plural of cherub; the origin of the word is uncertain, possibly from Akkadian karibu, 'one who prays or intercedes'.
entities.summary_bio: Winged heavenly guardians whom God stations east of the garden of Eden, with a whirling flaming sword, to guard the way to the tree of life after the man and woman are expelled.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew adamah, 'ground, arable soil'; related to adam, 'the man', in a wordplay.
entities.summary_bio: The soil from which the man was taken and to which he will return. The LORD God curses it because of the man, so that it yields thorns and thistles and bread only by toil.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew nachash, 'serpent'; related to a root for divination or hissing, probably, and wordplay with 'arum' (shrewd) in 3:1.
entities.summary_bio: A creature of the field, described as the shrewdest of the animals the LORD God made. It speaks to the woman, contradicts God's warning and leads her to eat the forbidden fruit. God curses it to crawl on its belly and sets enmity between its offspring and the woman's.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 3:7: they sewed fig leaves and made loin coverings.
Gen 3:21: the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and clothed him.
Gen 3:23-24: sent out from the garden of Eden and driven out.
Gen 3:10: 'I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself.'
Gen 3:23: sent out to till the ground from which he was taken; 3:17-19 toil.
Gen 3:7: 'they knew that they were naked'; 3:10 repeats it.
Gen 3:17: 'cursed is the ground because of you.'
Gen 3:14: 'cursed are you above all livestock and all beasts of the field.'
Gen 3:24: cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life.
Gen 3:7: they sewed fig leaves and made loin coverings.
Gen 3:21: the LORD God made garments of skin for his wife and clothed her.
Gen 3:23: God sent 'him' out; his wife, who shares the sentence and the garments, leaves with him (inferred).
Gen 3:16: 'your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you.'
Gen 3:20: the man called his wife's name Eve.
Gen 3:7: 'they knew that they were naked' and covered themselves.

systems.name: Divine curse
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East a curse was a binding pronouncement, often backed by a deity, that placed its object under a lasting disadvantage. Biblical curses (arur) are spoken by God or by those with authority and are effective.
rules_and_mechanics: Pronounced by the one with authority, here God himself.
Often introduced by a stated cause ('because you have done this').
Names a lasting consequence on the cursed party or thing.
Can fall on non-human things, such as the ground.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The man calls his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living.
system_instances.significance_note: Naming marks the man's authority and hope for life after the judgment.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The ground is cursed on account of the man and will bring forth thorns and thistles.
system_instances.significance_note: Only the ground is called cursed (arurah); the man himself is not, but bears the consequence.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God tells the man he will eat bread by the sweat of his face, until he returns to the ground from which he was taken.
system_instances.significance_note: Turns the man's work in the garden into hard labour and states the limit of human life: dust to dust.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God multiplies the woman's pain in childbearing and says her desire will be for her husband, who will rule over her.
system_instances.significance_note: Marks a change in the woman's condition after the fruit; childbirth and marriage are affected.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The serpent is cursed above all animals, condemned to go on its belly and eat dust, and enmity is set between its offspring and the woman's.
system_instances.significance_note: The first curse in the Bible; verse 15 is read in Jewish and Christian tradition as pointing to a future struggle between humans and evil.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The man and his wife hear the LORD God walking in the garden in the evening breeze and hide among the trees.
system_instances.significance_note: The first sign of broken fellowship: where God's presence was welcome, it now provokes fear.

edges.description: The man blames the woman God gave him for giving him the fruit.
The man names his wife Eve, mother of all the living.
The serpent tells the woman she will not die and that eating will make her like God.
The serpent asks the woman whether God really said they could not eat from any tree of the garden.
The woman says the serpent deceived her.
The woman gives her husband the fruit and he eats it.
The LORD God calls to the man and asks where he is.
God makes garments of skin and clothes the man.
God makes garments of skin and clothes the woman.
God curses the ground because of the man.
God curses the serpent above all animals for what it did.
God sends the man out of the garden of Eden to till the ground.
God stations the cherubim and the flaming sword east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.
God tells the man he will eat by toil until he returns to the dust from which he was taken.
God multiplies the woman's pain in childbearing and places her under her husband's rule.
God puts enmity between the serpent and the woman and between their offspring.
